newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines central bank says bullish on economy.
newsitem.headline: Philippines central bank says bullish on economy.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank said on Thursday the country was in a strong and healthy financial position and that economic growth was poised to outpace inflation in 1997.

"The strong economic results achieved in 1996 have by now clearly established the ability of the economy to stay on a high growth path without necessarily running into financial imbalances," said a report distributed by the bank.
The Philippine economy was waylaid by external shocks in the mid-1970s and early 1980s which drained its foreign exchange reserves.

In the year-end report to President Fidel Ramos, Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson said the country's balance of payments were expected to reach a $4.0 billion surplus by the end of the year from $631 million in 1995 following the heavy influx of foreign investments and loans.
Gross international reserves were projected to reach a record high of $11.5 billion this year, up 47 percent from the level achieved by the end of last year, he added.

Singson, however, said the current account deficit would widen to 4.2 percent of gross national product (GNP) from 2.6 percent last year, but assured the president that it was still one of the lowest in the region.
Nevertheless, exports had remained strong with growth expected to reach 17 percent or a total of $20.5 billion in value terms by the end of the year.
The bank also said inflation was expected to be about 8.5 percent in 1996 while GNP is expected to grow by more than 7.1 percent.
In 1997, however, the bank predicted GNP growth would outpace inflation for the first time since 1987. It said inflation was forecast at 6-7 percent in 1997 with GNP seen growing at 7-8 percent.
Singson said the healthy financial system has benefited from a series of liberalisation and deregulation measures adopted in the past years.

"With greater access to funds, banks and non-bank financial institutions increased their combined total resources to more than 2.0 trillion pesos (as of September 1996), or a 29.3 percent growth versus a year ago," Singson said.
He said there was no major bank failure during the period. "And taking into account all types of banks, for the first time in recent memory more banks were opened than closed," he added.
Peso savings increased by 20.3 percent, while foreign currency deposits rose by 30.4 percent in the year to September, the cental bank governor added.

"While the liberalisation of the economy has opened up multiple opportunities for rapid economic growth, it has also made it more vulnerable to sudden shifts in market sentiment that can cause sudden crises in the financial and foreign exchange markets," Singson said.
"The Central Bank is therefore committed to acting swiftly and independently to modify monetary policy, if the situation so warrants."
World Bank resident representative Vinay Bhargava said the country's economy is on a surer footing due to the series of structural reforms undertaken in the past years.
"If you look at the 1996 performance of the Philippines, it is clear that the Philippines is emerging as one of the star performers within the East Asian region," Bhargava told Reuters.
